title: Why the 'good old days' of American manufacturing are long gone

segments: Why manufacturing jobs left the US
summary.headline: Why US manufacturing jobs aren't returning; the path to a new industrial strategy
summary.tldr: Despite political promises that tariffs would bring manufacturing jobs back to the US, high labor costs and global supply chain efficiencies make this unlikely. Instead of chasing low-cost assembly, the US can pursue a manufacturing renaissance by focusing on high-tech sectors and building trade alliances.

key_points.point: US labor costs are significantly higher than in manufacturing hubs like China, often estimated at five times higher.
key_points.why_it_matters: High labor costs make it economically unfeasible to bring back mass-assembly jobs for products like furniture or consumer electronics.

key_points.point: Tariffs on China led companies to shift production to other low-cost countries like Vietnam rather than moving factories to the US.
key_points.why_it_matters: This demonstrates that companies prioritize low labor costs over domestic production when faced with trade barriers.

key_points.point: Willy Shih suggests the US should focus on maintaining leadership in high-value industries like jet engines, semiconductors, and biotech.
key_points.why_it_matters: Focusing on specialized, high-tech manufacturing allows the US to compete based on innovation rather than competing on labor costs.

key_points.point: The US could benefit from forming trade alliances with a wider network of countries to secure critical resources and labor.
key_points.why_it_matters: Building a collaborative trade block provides a more resilient and efficient supply chain than attempting to be self-sufficient.

numbers.context: The estimated ratio of US labor costs compared to those in China.

summary.lesson: When a country has high labor costs, it cannot compete on price for labor-intensive goods; it must instead focus on high-value, capital-intensive industries where innovation and specialized technology provide a competitive advantage.
opinions_and_predictions: Willy Shih (Harvard professor) believes the manufacturing jobs of the mid-1900s are not coming back to the US.
Willy Shih (Harvard professor) predicts that a manufacturing renaissance is possible if the US focuses on strategic, high-tech sectors and broader trade alliances.

glossary.definition: Taxes imposed by a government on imported goods.
glossary.example: The US government placed tariffs on goods from China to discourage imports.

glossary.definition: The entire network of entities, people, and processes involved in moving a product from raw material to the final consumer.
glossary.example: Furniture components might be sourced in New Hampshire, sawn in Vietnam, and assembled in China before reaching the US.

glossary.definition: Materials that conduct electricity under certain conditions, essential for modern electronics like computers and phones.
glossary.example: The US aims to maintain global leadership in the production of advanced semiconductors.

summary.quality_note: The content features an expert academic perspective on industrial economics, though the discussion on policy outcomes is framed as an analytical assessment rather than a neutral report.
